chapters.title: Dedication
paragraphs: To the people who keep a hotel alive while everyone else sleeps.

To the front desk agent who is still smiling after the last guest took out a bad travel day on them. To the housekeeper who knows a room is not ready before the inspector reaches the bathroom. To the engineer who hears a noise nobody else notices. To the night auditor who sits alone with the numbers after the building gets quiet. To the breakfast attendant who knows the real occupancy before anybody opens a report.
And to my brother, Juan Carlos, who taught me the lesson underneath almost everything in this book: love the people before you love the business.

chapters.title: A Note About the Stories
paragraphs: The lessons in this book are real. So are the mistakes.

Some scenes compress more than one property, more than one year, or more than one version of the same problem. Timelines, identifying details, job titles, and property characteristics have been changed when needed to protect the people and places involved. I am not interested in exposing a hotel, a company, an owner, or an employee. I am interested in exposing the work.
If a scene feels familiar to you, that is probably because hospitality repeats itself in different buildings.
The room number changes. The lesson usually does not.

chapters.title: Before We Start
pullQuotes: This business is actually a hell of a ride.
paragraphs: I did not enter hospitality because I had a career plan.
I entered because I needed a job.

I was eighteen, new to the United States, and still figuring out what version of my life had survived the move. Before that, soccer had been the center of everything. Then aviation looked like the future. Life had other plans. My family needed help, I needed income, and an opportunity came along at a hotel.
I thought I was going to work in an office.
Technically, I did.
The office just needed to be cleaned first.

I started as a houseman. I moved trash, linen, supplies, whatever the day needed. Later I worked security with a flashlight and a radio. None of it sounded impressive, and that is exactly why it was such a good education. I was close to the work before I had enough authority to misunderstand it.
I watched the building change personality by the hour.

At six in the morning the lobby belonged to coffee, luggage, airport runs, parents trying not to wake their kids, and business travelers looking at their watches. By three in the afternoon it was keys, arrivals, room status, early check-ins, lines, ringing phones, and that controlled panic every hotel operator knows. At eleven at night the lights looked the same, but the building felt different. Fewer voices. More exceptions. More truth.
That rhythm hooked me before I knew I was falling in love with the industry.

Hotels are strange businesses. Almost every part of human life eventually walks through the front door. Weddings and funerals. Vacations and divorces. Job interviews. Hurricanes. Canceled flights. A child's first trip to the ocean. A family sleeping somewhere unfamiliar because something went wrong at home. Two guests can be standing in the same lobby on the best and worst day of their year.
The guest sees one building.
Behind it is an entire economy.

Housekeeping is trying to turn yesterday into today. Front desk is translating every department into one human interaction. Maintenance is trying to keep the physical asset from aging faster than the capital plan. Revenue is deciding what tonight is worth. Sales is trying to create next month's demand. Food and beverage is balancing generosity, labor, waste, speed, and experience. Finance is explaining last month. Ownership is thinking about the next several years. And somewhere in the middle, the general manager is supposed to make all of those time horizons agree.
For a long time I thought getting better at hotel management meant learning more things.

Learn the property management system. Learn the reports. Learn the standards. Learn housekeeping. Learn labor. Learn revenue. Learn maintenance. Learn food and beverage. Learn sales. Learn finance. Learn ownership. Learn how to hire. Learn how to coach. Learn how to fire. Learn how to open a hotel. Learn how to fix one. Learn how to survive a bad month. Learn how to explain one.
All of that matters.

But after enough years, enough mistakes, enough openings, enough broken teams, enough good teams, enough guest complaints, enough owner calls, enough rooms not ready at three, enough numbers that did not tell the whole truth, the business became simpler in my head.
You need to understand two things.
Understand the people.
And understand the business plan of the property.
If you understand the people but not the business, you can build a place everyone loves working in that slowly runs out of money.
If you understand the business but not the people, you can hit a budget for a while and destroy the team required to hit the next one.
When you understand both, the chaos starts connecting.

A late room is not just a housekeeping problem. It may be a forecasting problem, a staffing problem, a linen problem, an elevator problem, a maintenance problem, a communication problem, a sales promise, or a leadership problem. A labor overage is not automatically bad management. Maybe the hotel picked up above forecast and the extra hours protected revenue. A guest complaint is rarely only about the thing the guest says first. An owner asking about one expense line is rarely only asking about the expense line. A team member who looks unmotivated may be lazy, yes. Or they may be confused, burned out, poorly trained, afraid to make a decision, disconnected from the purpose of the job, or working inside a system that makes good performance unnecessarily hard.
Once the pieces connect, something changes.
You stop fighting hospitality.
You start reading it.

This is not an SOP. I am not going to give you seventy-three steps for checking a room and pretend that makes you an operator. Checklists have a place. Standards have a place. Systems have a place. But a checklist cannot tell you which problem matters most at 4:15 on a sold-out Saturday when two people called out, the elevator is slow, a group arrived early, and your forecast missed pickup by twelve rooms.
That requires judgment.
Judgment is built from context.
This book is about how I learned the context.
Not from the executive office down.
From the floor up.

I want someone new to this industry to finish these pages understanding what business they actually joined. I want a supervisor to understand why the GM is staring at labor while the lobby is full. I want a GM to remember that the person cleaning a room may understand the operation in a way no dashboard can. I want an owner-minded operator to see that guest experience and asset value are not competing ideas. I want the person who has been in this business twenty years to recognize the smell of the back hallway, the 3:00 p.m. pressure, the quiet after midnight, and the truth that the building always knows before the report does.
The problems do not disappear when you get good at this.
You just stop expecting them to.
You get faster at identifying which problem is real, which one is noise, which one can wait, which one will compound, and which one needs you right now.
And if you stay curious long enough, you learn something else.
This business is actually a hell of a ride.
The point is not to make it calm enough that nothing happens.
The point is to understand it well enough to enjoy what happens next.

chapters.title: Learn the Building
chapters.tagline: The floor will teach you what the report cannot.
pullQuotes: The building always knows the truth before management does.
When nobody owns a decision, the decision does not disappear. It takes up space.
paragraphs: The first thing hospitality taught me was that the job description is almost never the job.
A houseman looks simple on paper. Public areas. Trash. Linen. Supplies. Help housekeeping. Keep the back of the house from turning into chaos.
In reality, the houseman is one of the few people who touches almost every department without belonging fully to any of them.

You see the room that keeps coming back dirty because the stain will not come out. You see the front desk agent trying to calm a family whose room is not ready. You see the engineer walking faster than usual and know something is up before the radio says it. You learn which deliveries arrive through which door, which elevator slows down under load, which supervisor helps when the shift gets ugly, and which person disappears the second the lobby fills.
I did not know I was learning operations. I thought I was working.
That is how a lot of the best hotel education happens.
You learn before anybody gives the lesson a name.
Later, working security, I learned something else: the hotel changes when management goes home.
During the day, weak systems can hide behind activity. There are enough managers, enough emails, enough people walking quickly enough that a broken handoff can survive until somebody patches it.
At night the building gets quieter, and quiet is honest.

A door that never latches properly becomes obvious. A noise complaint that nobody followed up on comes back. A guest who was mildly irritated at six can be furious by midnight because three people promised three different things and nobody owned the end of the story. A light that has been out for two weeks suddenly matters because there is nobody around to make the hallway feel safer.
That is when I started believing something I still believe now:
The building always knows the truth before management does.
The question is how long it takes management to hear it.
When I wanted to move to the front desk, my English was not ready. That was the answer I received, and it was fair. So I learned from the edge of the desk instead.

I printed registration cards. I learned how keys were made. I listened to the language experienced agents used when they did not have the answer a guest wanted. I watched a good agent handle a line of twenty people without making the twentieth person feel invisible. I watched another person make one difficult interaction infect the next five check-ins.
That is when I learned the front desk is not really a desk.
It is the switchboard for the entire hotel.
Every weakness eventually finds its way there.
A room is not ready? Front desk problem.
The air conditioner is not cooling? Front desk problem.
Breakfast closed earlier than the guest expected? Front desk problem.
The shuttle is late? Front desk problem.
The rate is wrong? Front desk problem.
The pool is closed? Front desk problem.
The department rarely owns every cause, but it almost always owns the first human reaction.
That is why guests do not experience departments the way we organize them.
We love org charts because they make accountability look clean.
The guest sees one hotel.
If housekeeping, front office, engineering, sales, and food and beverage act like separate companies, the guest becomes the person integrating them for you.
That is a terrible operating model.
My real education in the business side came from night audit.
Night audit gave me something rare in hotels: uninterrupted time with the data.
The building was quiet enough for me to ask stupid questions without an audience.
Why did that rate post differently?
Why was this room still out of order?
Why did occupancy change from the report I saw earlier?
Why does the number of rooms sold not feel like the number of people I saw in the lobby?
Why are we showing revenue in one bucket when the guest clearly bought something else?
What exactly happens between a reservation entering the system and the money showing up in the financial statement?

I ran reports because I was curious, not because somebody assigned them. I clicked into places people told me not to worry about yet. I learned how the property system thought, and once I understood that, the hotel stopped looking like departments and started looking like one connected machine.
A room begins as inventory.

Demand gives that inventory value. Revenue strategy decides what price makes sense. A reservation converts inventory into expected revenue. Housekeeping creates the physical product. Front desk turns the reservation into a human experience. Maintenance protects the product. Sales influences who will occupy it later. Food and beverage, parking, transportation, retail, events, and other outlets change the total value of the guest in the building. Night audit closes the loop and tells tomorrow whether today was recorded honestly.
That last part matters more than people think.
Night audit is not the shift where someone presses a button at the end of the day.
It is the moment the hotel decides what version of the day becomes history.
A weak night audit does not only create accounting errors. It sends bad information into tomorrow.

If room status is wrong, housekeeping starts with the wrong picture. If payment exceptions are unresolved, front desk inherits a problem. If rate exceptions are not understood, revenue sees noise. If the reports are technically complete but nobody verified what matters, management gets a packet that looks professional and still lies.
I have learned not to be impressed by a report packet just because it is thick.
The question is whether it tells the truth.
That principle follows me everywhere.
A dashboard can say the building is fine while the back hallway tells a completely different story.
I once spent an afternoon walking storage rooms floor by floor at a property that looked, from the lobby, like it was operating normally.
The storage rooms told me more than the lobby did.

One floor had clean linen mixed with discarded furniture. Another had supplies with no clear home. Old equipment was still being stored because nobody wanted to make the decision to throw it away. Extra clocks. Random lamps. Open boxes. Items ordered by people who no longer worked there. Things moved from one closet to another until the building became a museum of postponed decisions.
That is not a storage problem.
That is management made physical.
When nobody owns a decision, the decision does not disappear. It takes up space.
The same thing happens with maintenance.
Walk enough mechanical rooms and you learn that equipment almost never fails the day the problem begins.
There is usually a sound first. A leak. A vibration. A temperature change. A workaround. A part that is difficult to source. A team member saying, “We have been watching that.”
By the time the guest knows, the building has often been talking for weeks.
That is why walking the property is not theater.
I do not walk because I need people to see the GM walking.
I walk because email is edited reality.
The floor is less polite.
The report can tell you rooms are behind.
The hallway can tell you why.
Maybe carts are missing.
Maybe linen is late.
Maybe one elevator is slowing the entire vertical flow of the building.
Maybe a supervisor is cleaning rooms because two people called out.
Maybe maintenance has three rooms down for issues that could have been resolved differently.
Maybe the forecast was wrong and housekeeping was scheduled for the hotel we expected instead of the hotel we actually got.

I have had mornings when the forecast said one thing and pickup said another. By the time the team arrived, the operation had changed. You can protect the labor number and pretend the schedule is sacred, or you can protect the business that created the labor number in the first place.
Sometimes the right decision is to call in another housekeeper.
Then you explain the payroll later.
That is what understanding the building gives you: context to defend the right decision.
Without context, managers become loyal to plans after reality has already moved on.
A forecast is a plan.
It is not a commandment.
The same is true of room productivity.
People love a clean number because a clean number makes management feel controlled. X minutes for a checkout. Y minutes for a stayover. A certain number of rooms per person. Fine. You need standards.
But room productivity is not only time inside the room.

It is travel between rooms. It is waiting for linen. It is elevators. It is supplies. It is late checkouts. It is room mix. It is deep cleans. It is maintenance interruptions. It is whether the supervisor can inspect fast enough to release inventory. It is whether the front desk understands that “clean” and “ready” are not always the same thing.
If you only manage the number, you will eventually punish the wrong person.
That is why the best operators I know can move between the report and the floor without treating either one as complete.
They know the number matters.
They also know the number has a body.
There is another reason to learn the building before you try to lead it: every hotel has a different clock.

An airport property can feel like the morning begins before sunrise. The first wave of departures is tied to flights, not breakfast hours. A destination property can be quiet in the morning and explode in the afternoon. Extended stay has a different emotional relationship with the guest because the room is not just where someone sleeps; it becomes temporary home. A full-service hotel can have three different businesses happening under one roof before lunch. A small limited-service hotel can be harder than a larger one because there is nowhere to hide weak coverage. One person may be front desk, sales support, guest recovery, and the only person who knows where the extra key stock is.
Property type changes the rhythm.
Market changes the rhythm.
Guest purpose changes the rhythm.
Opening a hotel from scratch drove that lesson home in a completely different way.

Opening day is one of the few times you get to watch an operation become real in front of you. For months, the hotel exists as plans, deadlines, vendor lists, systems, hiring charts, brand requirements, construction meetings, and promises. Then one morning the doors open and all of those separate decisions have to become one guest experience.

The building can be ninety-something percent finished and still feel unfinished everywhere you look. A piece of furniture is missing. A system setting is wrong. A delivery is late. Somebody was trained on a process that changed yesterday. A room is physically complete but not operationally ready. There is always one thing nobody discussed because everyone assumed somebody else owned it.
The temptation before opening is to obsess over what guests can see.
The furniture.
The lobby.
The finishes.
The presentation.
Those things matter. But the opening taught me that the visible product is usually easier than the invisible operation.
Contractors can fix a wall on a schedule. Building a team that knows how to hand work to each other takes longer.

A beautiful lobby cannot compensate for a front desk team that does not know what to do when the first room is not ready. A perfect breakfast space does not matter if nobody forecasted production. A finished guestroom does not help if housekeeping, engineering, and front office do not agree on what “ready” means.
The first guest exposes the parts of the hotel that meetings cannot.

That is why mock operations matter more than they sound. Put real pressure on the system before a paying guest does. Let ten people arrive at once. Make a room fail inspection. Create a maintenance issue. Run breakfast as if the building is full. Follow a guest request from the first call to completion. Do not test whether people know their individual task. Test whether the handoffs survive.
The lesson stayed with me long after the opening.
Every hotel is reopening a little bit every day.
New employee. New shift. New group. New season. New manager. New system. New owner expectation. New room returned from maintenance. New process somebody swears will make everything easier.
The question is the same: does the operation work when separate pieces have to meet in real time?
That is why I do not trust a leader who walks into a new hotel and starts changing things before they understand who the hotel is for.
The first week should make you curious, not impressive.
What time do guests really wake up?
What do they complain about that never shows up in formal feedback?
Where does the line form?
Which department is always borrowing from another?
What happens when occupancy reaches the top of the range?
What breaks first?
What do employees warn each other about before a busy day?
Who does everyone call when something weird happens?
That last person is usually more important than the org chart says.
I have walked into hotels where the person with the most operational intelligence had the least impressive title in the building.

They knew why a certain room should never be assigned before noon. They knew which vendor could save you on a weekend. They knew which breaker fed the equipment that kept tripping. They knew which regular guest needed one small thing to become your biggest advocate. They knew the history behind the rule nobody understood anymore.
If you are the new manager and you do not find that person, you are choosing to learn everything the expensive way.
The building is full of teachers.
Most leaders are too busy talking to notice.
Learning the building also changes how you think about inspections.
A formal inspection is a snapshot.
The real inspection is every day.
If a scored visit reveals ten things that have obviously been wrong for months, the problem is not the inspector. The problem is that the operation became used to seeing them.
Hotels become blind slowly.

A damaged corner becomes background. A storage room gets a little worse every week. A breakfast setup carries one unnecessary step until that step becomes tradition. A front desk workaround that was supposed to last three days is still being used a year later. A temporary sign becomes permanent. A maintenance issue gets reset enough times that everyone stops asking why it keeps returning.
That is why fresh eyes matter.
But fresh eyes without operational understanding create another problem: activity for the sake of looking active.
I made that mistake in turnarounds early in my career. I walked in, saw visible problems, and started fixing them because fixing things feels like leadership.
Sometimes the most visible issue is not the important one.
The dirty closet might be a housekeeping issue.
Or it might be a purchasing issue.
Or storage design.
Or no par levels.
Or no supervisor ownership.
Or a vendor delivering quantities the building cannot store.
Or a manager who has been afraid to throw anything away because every purchase requires approval and nobody wants to admit the last order was wrong.
The point is not to make every problem complicated.
The point is to resist being impressed by the first explanation.
Hospitality trains you to move fast.
Experience teaches you when to slow down long enough to understand what you are looking at.
That is the first lesson of this book because everything else depends on it.
Before you manage the people, learn what their day actually feels like.
Before you challenge the labor, understand what the work actually requires.
Before you explain the P&L, understand what happened in the building that created it.
Before you add a system, understand the friction it is supposed to remove.
Before you blame a department, trace the handoff.
Before you send the email, walk the property.
You can become a manager without learning the building.
People do it all the time.
But you cannot become the kind of operator I trust that way.
That comes from enough mornings, nights, floors, reports, guest conversations, maintenance rooms, service elevators, storage closets, and ugly shifts that your instincts are no longer guesses.
The best operators are carrying a map in their head.
Not a floor plan.
A living map of how work, people, money, and time move through the property.
Learn that map first.
Everything else gets easier after that.

fieldNotes.title: Count the work at the moment it happens
paragraphs: Occupancy describes a hotel. It does not schedule one.

The same number of occupied rooms can be two completely different days. Departures pile the work up before arrivals. Stayovers spread it out. Long stays change the timing again. Guest count moves breakfast even when rooms sold do not.
You can get the daily total right and still build the wrong schedule.

Enough hours across the shift does not mean enough capacity before check-in. Housekeepers can clean faster than supervisors can inspect. Ready rooms can sit waiting on a slow release. Work finished after the guest needed it looks fine on the productivity report and does nothing for the person standing in the lobby.
The better question is simple.
How much work has to be done by each moment that matters, and what is slowing it down?
That question changes the conversation. You stop asking people to move faster. You start building a sequence they can actually deliver.
Hours buy capacity.
Timing decides if that capacity was worth anything.

chapters.title: People Are the Business
chapters.tagline: The numbers matter. The standards matter. None of them move without people.
pullQuotes: Culture is what people decide to do when nobody important is watching.
Care and standards are not opposites.
paragraphs: My brother taught me something before I had a management title: love the people before you love the business.
At first I heard it like family advice. Be decent. Treat people well. Do not become the manager everyone hates.
Years later, after leading teams that were great, teams that were exhausted, teams that were afraid, and teams that had forgotten why they cared, I understood the operational side of what he meant.
When leaders love the business first, people become instruments.
We need labor down, so they become hours.
We need rooms cleaned, so they become minutes.
We need scores up, so they become behaviors to correct.
We need a schedule covered, so they become bodies.
The problem is people can feel when they are being managed as inputs.
They may still clock in. They may still smile. They may still complete the checklist. But they stop giving you the part of hospitality that no staffing model can force: judgment.
The front desk agent who notices the guest does not need a policy explanation; they need the conversation to slow down.
The housekeeper who sees a child's stuffed animal and takes ten seconds to place it back carefully.
The engineer who hears something that is not technically a work order yet and checks it anyway.
The breakfast attendant who notices one family leaves early every morning and has coffee ready before they ask.
You cannot command that level of care into existence.
You create the conditions where people still want to give it.
That is culture.
Not posters.
Not a values statement nobody can remember.
Not pizza after a good inspection.
Culture is what people decide to do when nobody important is watching.
And one of the fastest ways to understand a hotel's culture is to watch what happens when something goes wrong.
Does the person tell the truth quickly?
Do they hide the mistake until they have a solution?
Do they blame another department before anyone asks?
Do they call a manager because they genuinely need authority, or because the culture taught them that making a decision is dangerous?
Do people help each other before somebody assigns them to?
Do they celebrate a win that belongs to another department?
That is the real culture survey.
I have inherited teams where everyone was polite and almost nobody was honest.
Those are harder than openly difficult teams.
Open conflict gives you something to work with.
Low-trust politeness gives you meetings where everybody nods, leaves the room, and has the real conversation somewhere else.
A hotel cannot move fast that way.
Bad news travels slowly. Help gets requested late. Small problems age into expensive problems because everyone is managing the reaction instead of managing the issue.
I care a lot about how quickly truth moves through an operation.
If something goes wrong at ten in the morning and I find out at four in the afternoon, the original problem may already be fixed. I still have another problem.
Why did six hours pass before the truth moved?
Maybe the employee was afraid of the manager.
Maybe nobody knew who owned escalation.
Maybe the manager has a habit of making every mistake feel like a character flaw.
Maybe the team has learned that the safest way to bring bad news is to wait until it comes with a solution.
Maybe the hotel is so used to working around the issue that nobody even recognized it as news.
Whatever the reason, the delay tells you something about leadership.
I try to remember that the first thirty seconds after someone brings you bad news teaches the entire team what to do next time.
That does not mean smiling at everything.
It means separating honesty from accountability.
“Thank you for telling me” can come before “This cannot happen again.”
Those sentences do not fight each other.
Care and standards are not opposites.
The strongest teams I have worked with had both.
People knew they mattered, and they also knew the work mattered.
That balance is harder than it sounds because every manager has a natural direction they lean when pressure goes up.
Some get softer. They avoid the conversation because they do not want to hurt the relationship.
Some get harder. They narrow the room until the only acceptable answer is the one already in their head.
I tend to move toward action.
I see the problem. I see the likely solution. I want to close the loop.
That quality helped me get promoted.
It also created some of my worst management habits when I used too much of it.
The danger with overusing something you are good at is that it does not feel like a problem from the inside.
It feels responsible.
You are not thinking, I am taking ownership away from my team.
You are thinking, I am making sure this gets done.
You are not thinking, I am shutting this person down.
You are thinking, We do not have time to debate this.
You are not thinking, Nobody wants to disagree with me.
You are thinking, We are finally aligned.
That is why self-awareness matters more as you move up.
Your intention is not the same thing as your impact.
I have had to learn that a leader can be right about the problem and still handle the moment badly.
A message as simple as “See me when you get in” can ruin somebody's entire drive to work if the relationship does not have enough trust underneath it.
A correction delivered three weeks late can be technically valid and operationally useless.
A leader who only appears when something is wrong will eventually make their presence feel like a warning.
People do not separate your words from the pattern they have experienced around them.
This is why recognition is not fluff.
Recognition tells people what the organization values before a mistake forces you to explain it.
The best praise is specific.
Not “good job.”
“You caught that before the guest had to ask twice.”
“You did not just move the room; you explained the handoff to housekeeping.”
“You saw the breakfast count was high and adjusted before we wasted another full pan.”
“You told me the truth before you knew how we were going to fix it.”
That last one matters.
If you want truth to move fast, recognize the people who move it.
The same principle applies to hard conversations.
Early in management I thought directness meant speed.
Say the issue. Say the expectation. Move on.
Now I think directness is respect, but only if you are direct about the right thing.
Behavior, not personality.
Impact, not insult.
Expectation, not vague disappointment.
And then listen.
That last part is the part managers skip when they already believe they understand what happened.
Sometimes you do understand.
Listen anyway.
Because the purpose of the conversation is not only to transfer information from your brain into theirs.
It is to understand whether the problem is unwillingness, inability, confusion, capacity, training, or something else entirely.
Those require different leadership.
The employee who does not know is not the same problem as the employee who knows and refuses.
The employee who cares but is overloaded is not the same as the employee who has checked out.
The employee who makes one mistake under pressure is not the same as the person creating the same risk every week.
If you treat all underperformance as attitude, you will lose good people and keep repeating bad systems.
People are expensive to misdiagnose.
I learned that again in properties that leaned too heavily on temporary labor.
Temporary labor can save an operation.
It can fill the board, cover the shift, protect a sold-out weekend, and keep a building functioning while you recruit.
But if too much of your operation is temporary for too long, you are not only renting labor.
You are renting culture.
You can train standards, but you cannot build deep ownership overnight with people who may not be there next week.
The permanent team sees it too.

They become the translators, the fixers, the people carrying the institutional memory while new faces rotate through. Eventually your strongest employees are not only doing their own jobs; they are absorbing the inconsistency around them.
That is when labor that looks flexible on paper starts costing more than the invoice says.
The same thing happens with leadership vacancies.
An empty management position does not create a clean hole in an org chart.
Its work leaks.
Some goes upward to the GM.
Some falls sideways to a supervisor.
Some disappears because nobody realizes it belonged to the role until it stops happening.
The natural response is to hire a title as fast as possible.
Experience taught me to slow down and ask a different question:
What work actually needs ownership?
Sometimes the answer is another manager.
Sometimes it is a stronger supervisor with a clearer lane.
Sometimes the org chart has more titles than the operation needs and fewer capabilities than the operation needs.
I care less now about what someone was called at their last job and more about what they can actually own.
Can they lead a shift?
Can they read the business?
Can they train?
Can they handle a guest without turning every issue into a GM issue?
Can they hold a standard and still keep the team with them?
Can they tell me I am wrong?
That last one is not a joke.
If every person in leadership agrees with the GM all the time, one of two things is happening.
You hired clones.
Or people have decided disagreement is not worth the risk.
Neither one is healthy.
I want managers who can say, “I do not think that will work, and here is why.”
Then we can argue about the business instead of managing politics.
But you cannot ask for honesty and punish it when it arrives.
That is where leadership consistency matters.
A lot of managers want open communication in theory.
Then somebody challenges the schedule, the labor plan, the room sequence, the promotion decision, or the GM's idea, and suddenly “open communication” has terms and conditions.
Your team notices.
The first month with a new team is especially important because everybody is studying you before they believe you.
They are watching what you inspect.
Who you greet.
Whether you remember what they told you.
Whether the rules change depending on who broke them.
Whether you help when the building gets ugly or disappear into email.
Whether you make a big show of listening and then do exactly what you planned anyway.
Whether you blame the previous team for everything you inherit.
Whether your promises survive the first hard week.
Leaders often walk into a new property wanting to prove they can improve it.
The team is asking a more basic question.
Can I trust you?
That is why the first thirty days are not mainly about proving intelligence.
They are about earning the right to influence.
Walk.
Listen.
Ask what is hard.
Ask what keeps breaking.
Ask what management does not understand.
Then do something with what you heard.
Nothing kills trust faster than collecting feedback you never use.
People are not stupid. They know when leadership is doing theater.
There is another part of people leadership nobody talks about enough: progression.
Employees stay where they can see movement.

Not everybody wants a promotion. Movement can mean learning, schedule stability, more money, a better shift, being trusted with something important, having a manager who sees them, or simply getting better at the job without being treated like they are replaceable.
The definition belongs to the person.
One of the easiest mistakes a manager can make is assuming everybody wants what they wanted.
I was ambitious early. I wanted to learn everything. I positioned myself around the front desk before I worked the front desk. I ran reports nobody asked for. I wanted the next thing.
That does not mean every good employee wants management.
Some want mastery.
Some want predictability.
Some want to go home to their family without carrying work in their head.
A good leader does not make everybody climb the same ladder.
They understand what progress looks like for the person in front of them.
That is what “love the people before the business” grew into for me.
Not softness.
Not avoiding accountability.
Not turning the hotel into group therapy.
It means remembering that every business result is being produced by human beings who are deciding, consciously or not, how much of themselves to invest in the work.
Your job is to make high standards feel worth carrying.
That requires clarity.
It requires consistency.
It requires real recognition.
It requires direct conversations before resentment builds around them.
It requires giving people enough room to make decisions and enough support to recover when a decision misses.
It requires being willing to keep someone in the game after a mistake instead of taking the ball back every time.
That last one was hard for me.
When you know you can solve the problem, doing it yourself feels efficient.
Sometimes it is.
But if you solve every problem your manager should be learning to solve, you are improving today's shift and weakening next month's operation.
The question I ask more often now is not, Can I fix this?
Of course I can fix a lot of it.
The question is, Should I be the one fixing it?
Sometimes the answer is yes.
A serious guest escalation. A safety issue. A legal risk. A capital decision. A people issue that belongs at my level.
But sometimes leadership means standing close enough to support the person without stealing the learning from them.
That is slower today.
It is faster later.
And that is the real game.
Not building a team that performs because you are always there.
Building one that knows what good looks like, knows why it matters, trusts the truth enough to say when something is wrong, and can move without waiting for you to become the answer.
Love the people before you love the business.
Not because the business does not matter.
Because the business is people.

fieldNotes.title: Coverage is a design decision
paragraphs: Payroll tells you what leadership costs.
It does not tell you when leadership is in the building.

Two structures can cost about the same and give the hotel completely different support. Put every decision-maker on the same hours and the hotel is heavily managed when it is quiet and thin when judgment matters most.
The org chart will not show you that.
Start with the decisions instead.
Who can release inventory?
Who can solve an exception?
Who can direct the team?
Who can check the condition of a room?
Who can make a commercial call?
When do those decisions usually show up? Which ones need someone physically in the building?
Then build the roles and the hours around that work.
One person does not have to own the strategy, inspect every room, approve every exception, and carry every shift. Those jobs can be split. They just cannot be split by accident.
Before you ask whether the hotel needs another manager, ask where authority disappears during the week.
The answer might change the schedule. It might change the job description. It might change who you hire.

chapters.title: Understand the Business Plan
chapters.tagline: You are not running rooms. You are running an economic model that happens to sleep people.
pullQuotes: Every department can be locally correct and globally wrong.
Eventually you realize the P&L is the hotel translated into money.
paragraphs: The first time I really understood rate management, I was working at a small hotel where every room mattered enough that you could feel a bad pricing decision by dinner.

There was no hiding behind a giant portfolio, a huge group base, or a complicated revenue structure. You could watch demand move in real time. You could see what happened when you held rate too long, dropped too quickly, sold the wrong room type, accepted business that looked good on the surface but blocked better business later, or filled the hotel without understanding what the occupancy was actually worth.
That property taught me something I wish every manager learned earlier:
A hotel is not a building with departments.
It is a business plan.
Everything in the operation is supposed to support that plan.
The problem is most employees never get shown the plan.
Sometimes managers do not fully understand it either.
They know their department.
Housekeeping knows rooms to clean.
Front desk knows arrivals and departures.
Maintenance knows work orders.
Sales knows accounts.
Revenue knows rate and inventory.
Food and beverage knows covers and cost.
Finance knows the P&L.
The GM is supposed to know how those pieces make money together.
That is different.
An airport hotel and a resort can use the same reservation system, the same accounting principles, and the same brand standards and still be completely different businesses.

The airport hotel may live on flight schedules, crew contracts, distressed passengers, short booking windows, shuttle capacity, early breakfast, and one-night stays. A destination property may live on weekends, weather, family travel, length of stay, leisure compression, and the emotional expectation that the hotel is part of the vacation, not merely where the guest sleeps. Extended stay has another model entirely. A guest staying twenty nights behaves differently, costs differently, complains differently, uses housekeeping differently, and evaluates value differently from someone there for one night.
If you do not understand why the guest chose your property, you do not understand the business yet.
That is where the business plan starts.

I have seen what happens when the operating model and the rate strategy drift apart. At one extended-stay operation, long-stay pricing had become more habit than strategy. The hotel could fill rooms and still leave money on the table because nobody had recently challenged whether the discounts, length-of-stay assumptions, and demand patterns still made sense.

Nothing looked dramatic at the desk. Reservations came in. Guests checked in. Occupancy looked healthy. That is what makes bad rate structure dangerous: the hotel can appear busy while the business quietly underperforms.

The fix was not simply “raise rates.” The first question was why the guest stayed that long, what alternatives they had, which dates actually needed the discount, how the stay affected housekeeping and inventory, and what the property was giving away in exchange for certainty.

The same thing happens with walk-in business. A front desk can accidentally create its own little revenue strategy if agents quote whatever rate is easiest, use the wrong booking path, or ignore the logic behind the channels the hotel is trying to manage. That is not just a front-desk training issue. It is a business-plan issue happening at the counter.
Who is the guest?
Why are they here?
What creates demand?
When does that demand appear?
How price-sensitive is it?
What does the guest use once they arrive?
What parts of the hotel create revenue, and what parts protect it?
What expenses are truly variable and what expenses only pretend to be?
What does ownership need this asset to become over time?
Those questions are more useful than memorizing a hundred KPIs.
The numbers matter, but numbers are only useful when they are attached to the operating model.
Occupancy is a good example.
People love occupancy because it feels intuitive. Full hotel, good. Empty hotel, bad.
Not always.

I have seen hotels celebrate occupancy that was bought too cheaply. I have seen teams protect ADR so aggressively that they gave up enough occupied rooms to damage total property economics. I have seen managers celebrate rooms revenue while breakfast cost per occupied room, bar volume, parking, and other ancillary revenue moved the other direction because there were simply fewer bodies in the building.
ADR and occupancy are not enemies.
They are two parts of the same decision.
The question is what combination creates the best result for the whole asset.
That phrase—whole asset—matters.
A hotel can optimize one line and make the property worse.
Rooms can win while food and beverage loses.
Labor can look good while guest experience deteriorates.
Marketing can spend more while demand quality gets worse.
Sales can book volume that pushes the wrong dates, wrong rates, or wrong mix into the building.
Maintenance can save expense today by delaying work that becomes capital tomorrow.
Every department can be locally correct and globally wrong.
That is why the GM has to understand the business plan better than the department plan.
One of the clearest examples for me has been labor.
Labor is emotional because it touches people and money at the same time.
A budget says how much labor the business should need at a certain level of activity. Fine.
But the schedule is written before the future becomes actual.
Demand moves.
Pickup changes.
Group patterns change.
Weather changes.
People call out.
Rooms stay occupied later than expected.
A maintenance issue creates extra work.
The hotel you scheduled on Thursday may not be the hotel you wake up to on Saturday.
I have had to call in additional housekeeping because actual rooms moved materially above forecast. On paper, that creates a labor variance.
In the building, it protects room readiness, guest experience, employee workload, and the revenue you just picked up.
The question is not, Did labor go over plan?
The question is, Did the additional labor produce or protect enough value to justify the decision?
That is business thinking.
A manager who is afraid of labor variance can make a financially worse decision while looking financially disciplined.
The reverse is also true.
“Business changed” cannot become permission to stop managing productivity.

You still need to know whether the extra hours were necessary, whether the work was sequenced correctly, whether people were productive, whether overtime could have been avoided, and whether the same surprise keeps happening because the forecast process is weak.
Context is not an excuse.
It is what makes accountability intelligent.
The same lesson applies to food and beverage.
I have worked in hotels where complimentary breakfast was treated like a brand requirement instead of a business operation.
That is how waste becomes invisible.

A buffet has demand forecasting, production, labor, purchasing, food cost, inventory, presentation, service, sanitation, and guest-experience decisions happening at the same time. The fact that the guest does not receive a check does not make the food free to the hotel.
A full pan thrown away every morning is not generosity.
It is a forecasting problem.
Running out early is not efficiency.
It is a guest problem.
Disposable supplies used without thought are not tiny expenses when they repeat every day across hundreds of guests.
The operator's job is not to squeeze the breakfast until guests hate it.
The job is to understand what the guest values and remove waste that adds nothing to that value.
Those are different things.
I learned to think about expenses this way across the property.
What is this dollar buying?
Sales labor. Advertising. Commissions. Guest supplies. Complimentary items. Overtime. Contract labor. Software. Equipment rental. Vendor services.
Every cost does not need immediate revenue attached to it, but it should have a business reason.
Activity is not return.
A sales department can be busy and unproductive.
A marketing campaign can create impressions and not create profitable demand.
A vendor can be familiar and still be too expensive.
A manager can work sixty hours and still spend most of those hours on the wrong things.
The business plan forces the question: what outcome is this supposed to create?
That is also how I learned to read a P&L.
At first, financial statements feel like school.
Rows. Variances. Percentages. Explanations.
Eventually you realize the P&L is the hotel translated into money.
The labor line is not a number. It is schedules, call-outs, productivity, staffing mix, overtime, management decisions, and forecast accuracy.
Guest supplies are not a number. They are purchasing discipline, waste, occupancy, service standards, and sometimes theft.

Repairs and maintenance are not a number. They are the age of the asset, preventive maintenance, emergency response, vendor pricing, deferred capital, and whether the team fixes things early or waits for failure.
Rooms revenue is not a number. It is demand, rate, room type, channel cost, length of stay, inventory discipline, reputation, sales effort, and the market's willingness to choose you.
A good GM should be able to look at a financial variance and walk backward into the building.
Not every answer will be obvious, but the questions should be.
Why did cost per occupied room move?
Why did flow-through weaken even though revenue grew?
Why did commissions rise without equivalent production?
Why is maintenance spending down while guest complaints about condition are up?
Why did occupancy outperform plan but profit miss?
Why did ADR grow while total revenue did not?
Those questions are where operations and finance stop being separate languages.
The best owner conversations I have had happened when I could tell the story before the report forced them to ask.
That matters because ownership does not only want good news.
They want predictability.
Bad performance is difficult.
Surprise bad performance is worse.

If I know the month is going to miss, I would rather explain what happened, what is structural, what is temporary, what I own, and what I am doing before somebody opens the report and builds a story without me.
That is part of operating with an ownership mentality.
Ownership mentality gets misunderstood in hotels.
Some people hear it and think: cut cost.
That is too small.
Thinking like an owner means understanding that today's operation is sitting inside a long-term asset.
A room out of order is not only a maintenance problem. It is inventory removed from sale.
A recurring leak is not only a repair expense. It may be future capital damage.
A damaged public area is not only a guest-experience issue. It affects reputation, brand pressure, future renovation scope, and how a buyer eventually sees the property.
A manager who ignores preventive maintenance may improve this month's expense line and make the ownership group poorer later.
That is not ownership mentality.
That is borrowing from the future.
I started understanding this more deeply as I sat in more conversations about capital.
Not every problem should be repaired forever.
Sometimes the equipment is past the point where labor can compensate for age.

I have seen teams spend extraordinary amounts of time keeping a failing system alive because replacement felt expensive. Daily cleaning. Temporary parts. Workarounds. Repeated vendor calls. Downtime. Guest impact.
Eventually you have to ask a more honest question:
Are we repairing an asset, or are we subscribing to its failure?
That is where capital planning becomes operational leadership.
The GM should know what is nearing end of life before ownership is surprised by it.
You do not need to be the engineer.
You need to know the risk.
What happens if this fails?
How much revenue does it touch?
Is the repair temporary or durable?
Are parts still supported?
What is the replacement horizon?
What other work should happen at the same time?
That knowledge makes you useful beyond the month you are managing.
It also changes how you think about inspections and brand requirements.
A required improvement can feel like somebody outside the building creating expense.
Sometimes it is exactly that.
But sometimes it exposes an asset issue the operation normalized because guests adapted around it.
The operator's job is not to complain about every requirement or blindly accept every one.
It is to understand the return, the risk, the timing, and the story.
What does this investment protect?
What does it improve?
What happens if we delay it?
Can the scope be smarter?
Does the work create a next chapter for the property or merely restore the last one?
That last question matters.
Great operators do not only keep hotels from breaking.
They see what the hotel could become.
A different use of space.
A better guest flow.
A stronger local food-and-beverage concept.
A more intelligent extended-stay rate structure.
A sales focus aligned with the property's real demand generators.
A service that removes friction guests repeatedly experience.
A capital project that improves both experience and operating efficiency.
That is value creation.
And it often starts on the floor, not in an investment model.
This is why I believe GMs should pay attention to the market beyond the front door.
What is being built nearby?
Which employer is growing?
Which one is leaving?
What competitor is renovating?
What property changed ownership?
What demand generator is weaker than last year?
What event pattern changed?
What flights changed?
What new restaurant, attraction, office, hospital, plant, school, or development will create or remove demand?
The market does not send a memo before it changes your business.
You have to stay close enough to notice.
But again, information is only useful when it connects to the business plan.
A piece of market news matters because it changes something.
Rate.
Occupancy.
Length of stay.
Segment mix.
Labor.
Capital.
Sales strategy.
Guest expectations.
That is the pattern I want every manager to learn.
Do not collect numbers.
Connect them.
Do not memorize that ADR is up.
Ask what happened to occupancy and total revenue.
Do not celebrate occupancy.
Ask what you paid to create it.
Do not complain about labor.
Ask what work existed and whether the schedule matched it.
Do not cut maintenance because the line is high.
Ask whether the spending is controlling risk or chasing failure.
Do not add a sales program because everyone else has one.
Ask what demand the hotel actually needs.
Do not manage the P&L as if the guest and the employee live outside it.
They are inside every line.
Once you understand the business plan, hotel management gets less mysterious.
Not easier.
Clearer.
You stop seeing isolated problems.
You see trade-offs.
You understand that a decision can be operationally correct and financially wrong, financially correct and culturally stupid, or perfectly reasonable in one property and disastrous in another.
That is why there is no universal “best practice” without context.
The best practice is understanding what business you are actually running.
Then making the building behave like it.

fieldNotes.title: The promise has a cost
paragraphs: A promise starts spending money the day you make it.

It decides which guest books. It decides the rate they accept. It decides how many people you schedule and what work they inherit. If those pieces do not agree, the difference ends up at the front desk.

Housekeeping frequency is the easy example. The model can make perfect sense on paper and still disappoint a guest who bought a different expectation. You can explain it in the welcome letter. That does not mean the guest read it. It does not mean they understood it. It does not mean they think it is fair for their stay.
So the question is bigger than communication.
What belongs in the base rate?
What can the guest ask for?
What work does that request create?
Who can deliver it every time?
Does the price pay for the experience you are selling?
Sometimes the guest misunderstood the promise. Explain it better.
Sometimes the promise is the problem. Change it.
Know which one is in front of you. Otherwise you keep paying for recovery on an expectation you keep creating.

fieldNotes.title: The amenity does not have to be yours
paragraphs: Not every part of the guest experience has to come from your own building.
Some properties cannot support another outlet, another kitchen, another vehicle, or another department. A local partner may already do the thing your guest needs, and do it well.
The contract is the easy part.
Follow one request from start to finish.
Who takes it?
Who sets the expectation?
Who gets paid?
Who delivers?
Who answers when something is missing?
Who can approve the fix?
Then follow the money through that same request. The commission is not the profit. Take out the payment fees, the time your team spends supporting it, the adjustments, and whatever you agreed to own.
Here is the part people forget. The guest found the service through you. When it goes wrong, they will come back to you. That is fair. Your name is on it even when someone else does the work.
A good partnership makes the guest's next step obvious and gives both businesses a reason to get it right, including on the day something goes wrong.

chapters.title: Fix the System, Not the Symptom
chapters.tagline: If the same problem keeps returning, stop admiring how well you solve it.
pullQuotes: Fix the leak before you buy a bigger bucket.
If the hotel only works because you are tired, you did not build a strong operation.
paragraphs: The first time I walked into a genuinely distressed operation, I did what ambitious managers do when they want to prove they belong there.
I started fixing things.
Fast.
Visible things.
Things ownership could see. Things employees would notice. Things I could point to at the end of the day and say, “That is better because I am here.”
Some of those things needed fixing.
I was still wrong about the job.
The visible problems were not the operation. They were evidence produced by the operation.
A dirty back office is easy to clean.
A culture where nobody owns the back office is harder.
A late room is easy to recover once.
A daily room-readiness problem means something underneath the room is broken.
A guest complaint can be solved with a conversation, points, a refund, an apology, or a room move.
A recurring complaint is no longer a guest-recovery issue. It is process data.
That distinction changed how I approach turnarounds, openings, and even good hotels that have one part of the operation slowly drifting.
Do not fix what you see first just because it is the first thing you see.
Ask what keeps producing it.
Hospitality rewards heroics too easily.
Someone stays late and saves the day.
The GM jumps behind the desk and clears the line.
The housekeeping supervisor cleans six rooms personally.
Engineering finds another temporary fix.
A front desk agent remembers the exception nobody documented.
The breakfast attendant goes to the store because purchasing missed something.
Everyone gets through the day.
We call that teamwork.
Sometimes it is.
Sometimes it is a weak system being carried by strong people.
Those are not the same thing.
A hotel can perform for months that way.

Great employees compensate for missing structure. Experienced managers remember what the process does not. People create side conversations, personal spreadsheets, text threads, sticky notes, and workarounds. The building functions because enough people know the unwritten version of how things really work.
Then one strong person quits.
Suddenly the operation looks broken.
It was already broken.
The person was the bridge.
That is why I pay attention to dependency now.
What stops if this person is off tomorrow?
What knowledge only exists in someone's head?
What exception only gets handled because one employee remembers to check it?
What report does everyone assume somebody else reviews?
What room issue is “known” but not actually recorded anywhere useful?
What guest promise depends on one manager being on property?
Those questions expose fragile operations fast.
I learned this especially well working with lean hotels.
In a small property, there is nowhere to hide confusion.

One person may cover three responsibilities. A manager may be part operations leader, part sales support, part purchasing, part human resources, part guest escalation. There may not be another layer to catch what gets dropped.
That environment taught me a lesson I carried back into larger hotels:
Clarity beats hierarchy.
You can have ten managers and still have no owner.
You can have four people and run beautifully if everyone knows what belongs to them, when it must happen, what “done” means, and when to escalate.
The easiest way to create micromanagement is to leave ownership vague.
Then the GM keeps checking because the system gives no reason to trust the work will surface on its own.
Did this get done?
Who followed up?
Did anyone call the vendor?
Was the guest contacted?
Are the rooms released?
Did we order it?
Did night audit catch the rate issue?
Did maintenance close the work order or only make the room usable?
When those questions live permanently in the manager's head, the manager becomes the operating system.
I have done that.
It feels productive until you realize the hotel gets weaker every time you rescue it from needing structure.
The goal is not to create more paperwork.
The goal is to make important work visible before it becomes urgent.
That is what good systems do.
A system is not software.
A system can be a five-minute morning conversation with the right information.
It can be a clean handoff between front desk and housekeeping.
It can be a predictable maintenance review.
It can be a weekly look at labor against actual demand.
It can be a simple rule that every unresolved guest issue has one owner until the loop is closed.
It can be the expectation that a room removed from inventory has a reason, a person, and a return-to-service plan.
The system is the repeatable behavior.
Technology should support it, not disguise that it does not exist.
I learned that the hard way because I love tools.

When you understand systems, technology is exciting. You can see exactly where manual work wastes time. You notice people copying the same information from one place to another. You see a front desk using paper for something that should be visible to multiple departments. You see managers chasing updates across group chats and emails while the actual operation is happening somewhere else.
My instinct was often to build something better.
Sometimes that was right.
Sometimes the technology simply made a bad process move faster.
That is not transformation.
That is efficient confusion.
Before adding any tool, I ask a question I wish more operators asked:
What exact friction are we removing?
Not “What features does it have?”
What work becomes easier?
What information moves faster?
What error disappears?
What decision improves?
Who owns it after launch?
What happens when the technology fails?
If you cannot answer those questions, the tool is probably becoming another place employees have to look.
Hotels already have enough places to look.
The strongest operating systems reduce the number of places truth can hide.
That is also why I stopped believing more checklists automatically create accountability.
A checklist can tell you somebody clicked complete.
It cannot tell you whether the work mattered.
It cannot tell you whether the standard was understood.
It cannot tell you whether the same box gets checked every day while the actual problem sits two feet away.
Verification matters.
But verification should be intelligent.
If an inspection repeatedly finds the same issue, the answer is not necessarily another inspection.
Maybe the standard is unclear.
Maybe training is weak.
Maybe the equipment is wrong.
Maybe the task is assigned to someone who cannot realistically complete it inside the shift.
Maybe nobody owns the correction after the finding.
Maybe the work order closes when the temporary fix is done instead of when the root cause is fixed.
Maybe the same failure should trigger training, not another reminder.
A hotel can drown in completed tasks and still fail to improve.
What matters is whether the loop closes.
That idea changed how I think about maintenance more than almost anything else.
A work order is not success.
A functioning asset is success.
Preventive maintenance is not success.
Reduced failure is success.
A deep clean is not success.
A room that stays at standard longer is success.
The activity is only useful if it changes the future.
This is why I like pre-mortems and post-mortems even if I do not use those words with the team.
Before something important: where could this fail?
After something important: what actually happened, and what should be different next time?
Hotels are full of repeat events.
Sold-out weekends.
Group arrivals.
Storms.
Holiday breakfast.
Inspections.
Renovation phases.
Month-end.
Employee turnover.
High-season transitions.
If the same type of difficult day teaches you nothing new each time, the operation is wasting pain.
One of the most useful habits I developed was fixing the worst recurring habit before adding a new initiative.
Managers love adding.
New meeting.
New form.
New incentive.
New training.
New metric.
New focus.
Sometimes the fastest improvement is subtraction.
Stop the bad booking path.
Stop the rate exception nobody can explain.
Stop letting rooms sit out of order without a daily decision.
Stop allowing unresolved guest issues to age across shifts.
Stop overproducing breakfast because “that is how much we always make.”
Stop storing broken equipment because nobody wants to decide whether to repair or discard it.
Stop scheduling to last month's habit when next week's forecast says something different.
Fix the leak before you buy a bigger bucket.
The reason this matters is operational debt.
Every tolerated workaround becomes a little debt.
The front desk learns a shortcut around a process.
Housekeeping learns to text one supervisor instead of updating the shared status.
Maintenance resets equipment instead of diagnosing why it trips.
Sales makes a promise the operating team will figure out later.
Night audit accepts a report exception because it always happens.
No single decision feels catastrophic.
Over time, the hotel becomes more dependent on memory and individual judgment to compensate for the exceptions.
Then the manager says, “Why is everything so hard here?”
Because you are paying interest on all the decisions nobody finished.
Cadence is one of the best ways to reduce that debt.
I used to think strong management meant knowing everything all the time.
That is impossible and exhausting.
Now I care more about knowing when important truth is guaranteed to surface.
There should be a rhythm to an operation.
Not meeting creep. Not filling the calendar until nobody has time to run the hotel.
A rhythm.
Certain things daily.
Certain things weekly.
Certain things monthly.

If I know we will look at room inventory every morning, labor against forecast every week, aging work orders on a set rhythm, and capital risk regularly, I do not need to spend all day scanning for every possible failure.
The system gives me scheduled moments to see the truth.
That is freedom.
Structure gets a bad reputation because people associate it with bureaucracy.
Bad structure is bureaucracy.
Good structure removes anxiety.
Everyone knows what happens next.
That is especially important when you are not physically there.
Managing across properties, helping a hotel from a distance, or supporting a manager who is developing taught me how quickly vague systems collapse when the GM is not in the building.
When you cannot walk over and ask, “Did this happen?” the process has to tell you.
That does not mean remote management through spreadsheets.
It means the on-site leader needs a clear operating picture and you need exceptions, not noise.
If everything is escalated, nothing is escalated.
The purpose of reporting is to help someone decide where attention belongs.
That is why I prefer a small number of meaningful signals over giant packets nobody reads.
Rooms at risk.
Labor materially off demand.
Guest issues not closed.
Maintenance affecting inventory or safety.
Cash or payment exceptions.
Rate anomalies.
Staffing gaps.
Anything that can materially change today's operation or tomorrow's result.
The point is not the list.
The point is the hierarchy.
The hotel produces thousands of facts.
Leadership needs the ones that change action.
This is also why one of my favorite questions is: who owns this, how often is it reviewed, and what action should happen when the number moves?
A KPI without an owner, a frequency, and an action is just a number.
It may look good in a dashboard.
It is not management yet.
The best systems also protect employees from unnecessary confusion.
If people regularly ask what the priority is, the operation has too many priorities.
If two managers give different instructions, the problem is leadership alignment before it is employee execution.
If a task belongs to “everyone,” it usually belongs to nobody.
If a standard changes depending on who is working, the standard does not exist.
Confusion is expensive.
It shows up as rework, overtime, frustration, guest inconsistency, turnover, and managers spending time resolving questions that should not exist.
The fix is rarely “communicate more.”
That phrase is too vague.
Communicate what?
Who decides?
Who owns?
By when?
What does good look like?
What can the employee decide without permission?
When does the issue move to the next level?
That is clarity.
And clarity is one of the kindest things a leader can give a team.
I have come to believe the strongest hotel operations are not the ones with the most rules.
They are the ones with the fewest mysteries.
People know what matters.
They know where truth goes.
They know what happens after a miss.
They know which decisions are theirs.
They know the rhythm.
They know the business reason behind the work.
And they know the manager will inspect the system without taking ownership back every time something goes wrong.
That last part is critical.
If you delegate and then grab the work back at the first imperfect result, you did not delegate.
You rented the task until you got nervous.
Development requires enough patience to let someone improve inside real responsibility.
The manager's job is to create the conditions, clarify the standard, coach the misses, and intervene when the risk truly requires it.
Not to become the permanent emergency contact for work other people should own.
A lot of strong operators struggle with this because the better you are at solving problems, the more the operation rewards you for continuing to solve them.
Everyone loves the manager who saves the day.
Until that manager takes a vacation.
Then everybody discovers whether there was a system underneath the hero.
That is the test.
If the hotel only works because you are tired, you did not build a strong operation.
You built a dependency with good numbers.
The next level of leadership is less impressive from the outside.
Fewer rescues.
Fewer dramatic saves.
More boring consistency.
Problems surface earlier.
People make more decisions without you.
The same issue stops returning.
The building becomes less dependent on who happens to be working that day.
That is what good operations feels like.
Not perfect.
Predictable enough that the unexpected does not destroy you.
And when something does break, you do not only ask, “How do we fix this?”
You ask the question that changes the future:
What allowed this to become possible?

fieldNotes.title: The score has two clocks
paragraphs: Guest feedback runs on two clocks.
One is when the stay happened. The other is when the comment arrived.

A review that lands today may describe a stay from before you fixed anything. A guest in the building right now may already be getting the new process and has not said a word. A rolling average carries both at the same time.
So the score lies a little. Not on purpose. It is just late.
Before you react, ask three things.
When did this stay happen?
What exactly is the guest describing?
Was the change actually in place?
Watch the sample size too. A handful of new responses can move an average without proving anything changed.
Then check the operation itself. Was the service delivered? Was the guest contacted? Did the same complaint come back?
A better process should earn a better score eventually. The gap between those two moments is where management needs discipline.
Without it, you kill a good change too early.
Or you celebrate a number the work has not earned yet.

chapters.title: Hold the Pressure
chapters.tagline: The job is not to eliminate pressure. The job is to keep it from becoming everybody else's problem.
pullQuotes: The leader should absorb complexity and return clarity.
paragraphs: There is a version of hotel management people imagine before they do it.
You walk the lobby. You greet guests. You lead the team. You review the numbers. You solve a few problems. You go home.
Then there is the actual job.
The room is not ready.
The guest has already waited.
The housekeeper called out.
The elevator is slow.
The vendor did not deliver.
A manager is upset.
Ownership wants an explanation.
The forecast moved.
A guest posted something online that makes the hotel sound like a crime scene.
And all of this can be happening before lunch.
Pressure is not a special event in hospitality.
It is part of the operating environment.
The question is what you do with it.
Early in my career, pressure made me faster.
That sounds like a strength, and sometimes it was.
I could make a decision while other people were still discussing the options. I could see what mattered, assign work, move people, and create motion.
The problem is speed is contagious.
So is anxiety.
A GM moving quickly through a calm building can make everybody assume something is wrong.
A sharp tone travels farther than the sentence that caused it.
A frustrated manager can make five people feel behind even when the operation is actually recoverable.
I had to learn the difference between carrying urgency and transmitting urgency.
They are not the same.
A serious problem may require a fast response.
It does not automatically require a frantic leader.
That distinction became especially clear to me in hotels where weather, travel disruption, or other external events suddenly changed the operation.

When flights cancel, the lobby can fill faster than the hotel can emotionally prepare for it. People arrive tired, hungry, angry, uncertain, and already disappointed by somebody else. The front desk becomes the first available human target.
At that moment, the property does not need the GM adding a second emergency to the first one.
It needs clarity.
Who is handling arrivals?
Who is watching room availability?
Who is communicating transportation?
Who is helping housekeeping?
What can we promise?
What can we not promise?
What information is changing, and who needs it?
The leader should absorb complexity and return clarity.
That sentence has become one of the simplest descriptions of the job for me.
The team does not need every worry in my head.
They need the part that changes what they should do next.
This matters with guests too.
One of the easiest mistakes in service recovery is defending the hotel too early.
A guest tells you what happened, and because you know the operation, your brain immediately starts producing explanations.
The room was inspected.
The item was fresh.
The engineer responded.
The front desk called.
The team followed procedure.
Maybe all of that is true.
It can also be the wrong first response.
The guest is not asking you to win a case.
They are telling you how the experience landed.
You can investigate without becoming defensive.

I have had guest complaints where the evidence inside the hotel pointed in a different direction from the guest's conclusion. The worst thing I could do in that moment was treat the conversation like a courtroom.
The better sequence was human first, facts second.
Acknowledge the discomfort.
Understand the impact.
Investigate the facts.
Take reasonable action.
Then explain what you know without making the guest feel stupid for what they experienced.
That is harder than issuing a scripted apology.
It requires confidence without ego.
Hospitality leaders spend a lot of time in situations where two things can be true at once.
The team may have followed procedure, and the guest may still have had a bad experience.
The employee may be a good person, and the behavior may still require discipline.
The owner may be right about cost pressure, and the proposed cut may still create operational risk.
The hotel may have missed budget, and management may still have made several correct decisions that prevented a worse result.
Mature leadership lives in those uncomfortable combinations.
Pressure makes people want simple villains.
Operations usually gives you systems, trade-offs, and incomplete information instead.
That is why I try not to make permanent judgments inside temporary emotion.

I have had career moments where somebody above me made a decision I believed was wrong. I have been frustrated by leaders who understood presentation better than operations. I have had assignments change, people leave, and situations end before I believed they should.
Those moments hurt more when you care about the work.
They can also distort your thinking.
You start rewriting the whole story around the last decision.
Do not do that.
One bad leader does not erase the people who taught you well.
One bad inspection does not mean the team is bad.
One bad month does not make you a bad operator.
One strong month does not make you a genius either.
Hospitality is humbling if you stay long enough.
The market will help you and let you think you did it.
Then the market will hurt you and let you think you caused everything.
The truth usually sits somewhere between ownership and humility.
Own what is yours.
Do not claim what is not.
That principle helps under financial pressure too.
There is a moment every GM knows when the report is going to be bad before the report is final.
You can feel the temptation to wait.
Maybe something improves.
Maybe an accrual changes.
Maybe the final numbers look less ugly.
Maybe nobody asks immediately.
Waiting almost never improves the trust side of the equation.
I would rather tell the story before the spreadsheet tells it for me.
Here is what happened.
Here is what was market.
Here is what was ours.
Here is what I should have seen earlier.
Here is what we changed.
Here is what I expect next.
That is not about sounding confident.
It is about being useful.
Ownership can handle bad news better than vague news.
Teams can too.
The same rule applies downward.
If the business is under pressure, employees will feel it before leadership decides what to say.
Hours change.
Managers act different.
Purchasing tightens.
Vacancies stay open longer.
People notice.
