Pretending everything is fine creates more anxiety than saying what is true at the level people need to know.
But transparency does not mean dumping every executive worry into the break room.
Again: absorb complexity, return clarity.
“This is the challenge. This is what we are doing. This is what I need from you. This is what is not changing.”
That is leadership under pressure.
The same principle became personal for me during some of the hardest operating periods of my career.
There were times when the hotel was performing and I was not okay.
That is a dangerous combination because external success can hide internal depletion.
You are still answering emails.
Still making payroll.
Still walking the building.
Still solving problems.
Still getting results.
From the outside, nothing looks broken.
Inside, there is less curiosity.
Less patience.
Less creativity.
You are running the same plays because they still work, not because you have energy to see a better one.
That is what burnout looked like for me.
Not collapse.
Continuation without renewal.
Hospitality rewards that for a while.
People call you committed.
Reliable.
A grinder.
The problem is a person can be operationally dependable and slowly become a worse leader.
You listen less.
You get irritated faster.
You use experience as a shortcut instead of a tool.
You stop exploring.
Everything starts feeling like another version of something you have already solved.
That is when you need to pay attention.
A depleted operator can still hit numbers.
That does not make the operating model sustainable.
I eventually stepped away from hospitality for a period and worked in a completely different world. At the time, it felt like interruption.
Later I understood it as recovery and education.

I learned more about technology, systems, digital business, customer behavior, and what other industries considered normal that hotels still treated like innovation. More importantly, I remembered what curiosity felt like when every problem was not already familiar.
When I came back, I came back differently.
Still an operator.
Less impressed by suffering.
That matters because hospitality has a weird relationship with sacrifice.
We celebrate the person who never takes a day off.
The manager who answers at midnight.
The leader who covers three departments.
The person who stays late every day.
Sometimes that is exactly what the moment requires.
Sometimes it is evidence the system is broken and the leader has made endurance part of the org chart.
There is nothing noble about being permanently exhausted by work you were supposed to organize.
You will have ugly weeks.
You will have seasons where balance is a joke.
Openings, storms, renovations, turnovers, peak periods, inspections, crises—some moments demand more.
But if emergency output becomes your normal identity, eventually the hotel will own everything you have.
And then you will have less to give the people who actually matter outside the building.
I have learned to think of energy the same way I think about capital.
You can spend aggressively for a period.
You cannot spend indefinitely without replenishment.
The goal is not a soft life.
The goal is longevity.
The best operator over ten years is not necessarily the one who can suffer the most this month.
It is the one who can keep judgment, curiosity, relationships, and standards intact over time.
That requires knowing when pressure is useful and when you are simply passing it along.
It also requires knowing what belongs to you.
As the leader, some hits should stop with you.
A guest screaming at a line employee because of a management decision? Step in.
An owner upset about a result the team produced under the strategy you approved? Own the strategy.
A manager who made a reasonable call inside the authority you gave them and got a bad outcome? Coach the decision, but do not disappear when accountability arrives.
Leadership is not taking credit upward and pushing pain downward.
People remember who stood beside them when the decision got expensive.
That does not mean protecting bad performance.
It means protecting honest ownership.
If I asked someone to make decisions, I cannot punish them for every decision that does not work.
If I want people to bring me bad news, I cannot make bad news emotionally dangerous.
If I want managers to own departments, I cannot overrule them casually in front of their teams.
Pressure reveals whether empowerment was real or decorative.
That is why hard periods are so educational.
Calm months let weak leadership hide.
Pressure exposes the structure.
Who communicates?
Who blames?
Who freezes?
Who quietly solves things nobody notices?
Who protects the guest?
Who protects only themselves?
Who tells the truth?
Who waits?
Who needs permission for everything?
Who can take a hit and stay useful?
You learn a lot about people in those moments.
You learn even more about yourself.
I have learned to ask one question when I can feel pressure narrowing me:
What does this moment need from me?
Not what do I feel like doing.
Not what would prove I am in charge.
Not what would make the anxiety disappear fastest.
What does the moment need?
Sometimes it needs a fast decision.
Sometimes it needs me to shut up and listen.
Sometimes it needs another housekeeper.
Sometimes it needs me to tell ownership the month will miss.
Sometimes it needs me to remove someone from the floor.
Sometimes it needs me to let a manager finish the decision I am tempted to take over.
Sometimes it needs me to go home before I become the worst weather in the building.
That question does not make leadership easy.
It gives pressure somewhere useful to go.
The hotel will keep producing contact.
Guests will complain.
Employees will disappoint you.
You will disappoint them.
Forecasts will miss.
Equipment will fail.
Owners will push.
Standards will move.
People will leave when you wanted them to stay and stay when you are not sure what to do with them.
That is not evidence you chose the wrong career.
That is the career.
The job is to keep advancing the operation without making every difficult moment feel like a crisis.
Hold the pressure.
Return clarity.
Then get ready for the next day.

fieldNotes.title: The next step is part of the service
paragraphs: Some of the hardest guest problems are the ones the hotel cannot fix.
The flight was cancelled. The third-party booking does not match. The card got declined by the bank. The decision belongs to another company.
Telling the guest it is not your department may be accurate. It is also where a lot of hotels stop being hospitable.

The guest is usually tired, stressed, sometimes working in a second language, and standing in front of the only person who looks like they might help. Telling them to call the provider is true and still leaves them stuck.
Precision is the service here.
Figure out what they are actually trying to get done.
Separate what you can confirm from what you cannot.
Tell them exactly who can take the next action.
Tell them what to ask for when they get there.
Hand them a phone, translate, write it down, if that is what it takes.
None of that means promising an outcome you do not control. Never do that.
Your authority ends somewhere. Say where, clearly.
Then point to the next door.

chapters.title: Enjoy the Ride
chapters.tagline: The chaos does not disappear. Your ability to read it gets better.
pullQuotes: You do not graduate from chaos.
Strategy that cannot survive contact with that reality is not strategy.
paragraphs: I used to think the people who had been in hospitality a long time must eventually reach a point where the job felt under control.
They knew the answers.
They had seen everything.
They had enough experience that very little surprised them.
That part is partly true.
The surprise changes.
The control does not arrive.
A hotel is too alive for that.

There are too many people, too many handoffs, too many systems, too much weather, too much demand movement, too many mechanical parts, too many personalities, too many financial pressures, too many reasons a guest may walk through the door.
You do not graduate from chaos.
You become more fluent in it.
That is different.
When I started, a line at the front desk looked like a front desk problem.
Later I learned the line may have started upstairs two hours earlier.

Rooms were not inspected quickly enough. Or housekeeping was short. Or pickup moved. Or early arrivals were promised too freely. Or a maintenance room stayed out longer than planned. Or a group bus arrived before the schedule. Or the elevator made every movement through the building slower.
Experience did not make the line disappear.
It gave me more places to look.
That is what this career has done to me over time.
It gave me more places to look.
At the beginning, I looked at the task.
Then I learned to look at the department.
Then the handoff.
Then the property.
Then the P&L.
Then the ownership perspective.
Then the market.
Then the person leading all of it, including myself.
The farther I moved from the first job I had in the building, the more valuable that first job became.
I still think about the houseman role because it taught me something titles can make you forget: the hotel is physical before it is strategic.
Somebody has to move the linen.
Somebody has to clean the room.
Somebody has to answer the phone.

Somebody has to reset the breaker, cook the eggs, deliver the towels, balance the accounts, move the guest, inspect the room, take the trash, unlock the door, and stand in front of a tired traveler who does not care how complicated the organization is behind the desk.
Strategy that cannot survive contact with that reality is not strategy.
It is presentation.
That belief shaped the way I eventually started thinking about technology too.
I did not become interested in systems because technology was fashionable.
I became interested because I got tired of watching good people lose time to bad processes.
Paper sign-up sheets.
Information living in one person's messages.
The same data copied into multiple places.
A guest calling the front desk for information the hotel already knew how to answer.
Managers chasing updates instead of managing exceptions.
Employees being blamed for missing a handoff that the process made unnecessarily fragile.
Once you see enough of that, you start asking a dangerous question:
Why are we still doing it this way?
That question matters even if you never build a piece of software in your life.
Operators should be builders.
Not necessarily builders of technology.
Builders of better ways.
A better shift handoff.
A better room sequence.
A better manager meeting.
A better hiring question.
A better way to show ownership what matters.
A better way to make the guest's next step obvious.
A better way to turn a recurring failure into learning instead of another apology.
The industry needs more people who understand the work deeply enough to redesign it without disrespecting the people doing it.
That last part matters.
There is a type of improvement that makes sense from far away and makes the job worse up close.
Every operator has seen it.
A new process adds three clicks to save management one question.
A report is created because one executive asked for it once, and now fifty people produce it forever.
A standard designed for consistency removes the judgment that made the service feel human.
A cost cut saves money in one department and creates twice the work somewhere else.
A technology rollout assumes the team has time, equipment, training, and connectivity that do not exist in the actual work environment.
That is why the people closest to the work should be part of changing the work.
Not because every decision needs a committee.
Because reality has a vote whether leadership invites it or not.
I have become more interested in this as my career has expanded beyond one building.
When you spend years running hotels, you eventually notice the same problems wearing different uniforms.
Disconnected information.
Training that exists but does not show up in execution.
Standards that depend on one strong supervisor.
Revenue decisions that operations does not understand.
Operations decisions that revenue never hears about.
Maintenance risks that live in engineering until they suddenly become ownership problems.
Guest feedback that gets reviewed after the guest has already told the internet.
Schedules written from habit instead of demand.
Meetings filled with information and empty of decisions.
The hotel changes.
The pattern repeats.
That was one of the moments when hospitality became bigger to me than a job title.
I started seeing the industry as a system with enormous room to improve.
But I also became more respectful of why it is hard.
Hotels are not factories with one product moving through a controlled line.
Every guest changes the product slightly.
Every employee delivers part of it differently.
The building itself ages while you operate it.
Demand changes daily.
The product expires every night.
An unsold room at midnight cannot be put back on the shelf tomorrow.
The workforce is labor-intensive by design because hospitality still requires humans at the moments where humans matter most.
And the experience must feel easy to the guest even when the operation behind it is extremely complicated.
That is beautiful when it works.
It is also why the job can become addictive.
There is a satisfaction in watching a building find rhythm.
Rooms are moving.
The desk is calm.
Breakfast is full without feeling crowded.
The engineer handled the issue before it became a complaint.
A manager made a decision without calling you.
A new employee finally gets it.
The guest who arrived upset is laughing with the agent ten minutes later.
The numbers close where they should.
Nobody outside the industry would look at that day and call it extraordinary.
Operators know.
That is a good day.
You should learn to enjoy those days because the industry is very good at training you to notice only what is wrong.
That is one of the occupational hazards of becoming experienced.
Your eye gets sharper.
You walk into a lobby and see the burned-out bulb before the flowers.
You see the line before the full house.
You see the labor variance before the revenue pickup.
You hear the complaint before the ten compliments.
You notice the one manager who missed the follow-up before the five things the team recovered without you.
That skill protects standards.
If you let it own you, it also steals the joy from the work.
I have had to learn to see what is working with the same discipline I use to see what is broken.
That is not positive thinking.
It is accurate management.
If the only feedback your team receives is about gaps, eventually they stop believing you can see progress.
If the only story you tell yourself about your career is what still needs improvement, eventually success becomes emotionally invisible.
A hotel is never finished.
Neither are you.
At some point, if you are not careful, growth becomes a reason to stay permanently dissatisfied.
The next property.
The next title.
The next project.
The next percentage point.
The next system.
The next problem to solve.
Ambition is useful.
It got me out from behind a mop, toward the front desk, into night audit, into management, into bigger responsibility, into rooms I never imagined I would enter when I first arrived in this country.
But ambition needs perspective or it turns every current life into a waiting room.
I do not want to live that way.
Hospitality taught me too much about time for that.
Every night the hotel sells inventory it will never get back.
Life is not very different.
You can waste a lot of good days waiting for the perfect one.
That realization became stronger when I stepped away from the industry and later returned.
Distance showed me what I missed.
Not the emails.
Not the reports.
Not the budget meetings.
I missed the building.
The movement.
The weirdness.
The fact that at any moment something completely human can interrupt the operating plan.
I missed being around people who know how to keep moving when the day does not cooperate.
Hospitality people are a strange group.
We complain about the chaos and then get bored when things are too quiet.

We say we want predictable days and then choose an industry where a fire alarm, wedding party, water leak, canceled flight, sick employee, celebrity arrival, broken elevator, sold-out weekend, and birthday cake request can all become relevant before dinner.
There is a reason many of us stay.
The work is alive.
The trick is learning to participate in that life without letting it consume yours.
A GM who becomes only a GM eventually runs out of things to bring into the role.
You need a life outside the building.
Family.
Friends.
Curiosity.
Something that has nothing to do with occupancy.
Something you are bad at.
Something that reminds you the hotel is important and still not the entire world.
That perspective makes you better inside the building too.
You react less like every bad day is a verdict on your identity.
You can make a hard decision without carrying it home forever.
You can support an employee without needing to become their entire support system.
You can care deeply about the asset without pretending the asset loves you back.
You can leave when the chapter is over without turning every ending into failure.
That is maturity I did not have early.
Early in your career, you think loyalty means staying.
Later you learn loyalty can also mean telling the truth, doing the work well, developing people, leaving the operation stronger, and knowing when your part is complete.
The industry is full of chapters.
Openings.
Turnarounds.
New teams.
New owners.
Renovations.
Promotions.
Departures.
Properties you save.
Properties that teach you more than you save them.
People you manage who later become peers.
People you thought would stay who disappear.
People you almost gave up on who become leaders.
The story is not clean.
That is what makes it worth telling.
If I had to reduce everything I know now to one operating philosophy, it would still be the same three ideas that eventually simplified the business for me.
Understand the people.
Understand the business.
Enjoy the ride.

Understand the people means know the guest before you design the service. Know the employee before you assume motivation. Know what your managers are carrying. Know how your own behavior lands. Know when someone needs clarity, when they need coaching, when they need accountability, and when they need you to get out of the way.

Understand the business means know why the property exists economically. Know what creates demand. Know what the room is worth. Know how labor should move with work. Know what maintenance protects. Know what the P&L is telling you. Know what ownership needs. Know which investment creates value and which expense is only habit. Know the difference between a busy hotel and a healthy one.
Enjoy the ride means stop waiting for hospitality to become something it is not.
It will be messy.
It will be human.
It will occasionally be ridiculous.
You will have days when everything you planned before breakfast becomes irrelevant by ten.
You will make decisions with incomplete information.
You will get some wrong.
People will remember your worst day and your best day differently than you do.
You will leave work exhausted from solving problems nobody outside the industry would understand.
And then you will come back.
If you do this well, something changes over time.
You stop needing to be the hero of every shift.
You build people who can think.
You build systems that carry the routine.
You save your energy for the decisions that actually require you.
You read the building faster.
You read the numbers deeper.
You take bad news with less ego.
You celebrate good work before moving immediately to the next gap.
You become less interested in proving you are the smartest person in the room and more interested in whether the room can perform after you leave it.
That is the kind of operator I want to keep becoming.
Not the person who knows everything.
The person who understands enough of the whole picture to help other people do their best work inside it.
Sometimes I think about the version of me walking a hallway with a flashlight and a radio.
He did not know what RevPAR was.
He did not know how to read a P&L.
He did not know about capital plans, labor productivity, channel mix, flow-through, guest segmentation, or any of the language that would later become normal.
He knew the building felt different at night.
He knew he was curious.
He knew he wanted to understand why things worked the way they did.
That turned out to be enough to start.
Maybe that is enough for anyone.
Stay curious about the building.
Stay close to the people.
Learn the business behind the work.
Be harder on broken systems than you are on human beings trying to survive them.
Tell the truth early.
Do not confuse suffering with leadership.
Do not let the hotel become dependent on your exhaustion.
Leave the operation stronger than your presence.
And every once in a while, when the lobby is moving, the rooms are ready, the team is laughing, the numbers make sense, and nobody needs you for five whole minutes, notice it.
That is the ride.
You are in it.
Somehow, you will manage.
— Alejandro Soria

fieldNotes.title: The upgrade has to earn its place
paragraphs: Every field you add to a screen costs somebody part of their shift.
Leaders forget that. A new report, a new required field, a new step in the system looks free from the office. At the desk it is one more thing between the agent and the guest.
A feature that helps management has to be weighed against the work it asks the team to do. If the team pays for it and nobody uses what it produces, it is not a feature. It is a tax.

Pay attention when people keep using the simple tool and ignore the new one. That is not resistance. That is information. They are telling you the old way already handles the job, and the new way has not earned the extra effort yet.
Start with the friction. What does the team repeat? What do they forget? Where does the guest wait? Which step eats everybody's attention?
Build around that.
Add the next thing only when a real, recurring need earns it.

fieldNotes.title: Decide where the saved time goes
paragraphs: AI can make routine work faster. It cannot decide what that time is for.
That is a leadership job.
When a report takes half the time it used to, you created capacity. Now you have three choices. Let it fill up with more reports. Let it disappear. Or put it somewhere on purpose.
That choice deserves as much attention as the tool.

In hotels, the best use of time is usually the work no software does well. Understanding why an employee made a call. Teaching a supervisor the economics behind a schedule. Noticing the guest who looks unsure. Talking through a tradeoff before it becomes an emergency.

There is a trap too. Better tools make it easier to produce an answer that sounds right without understanding it. A manager still has to question the assumptions, see what is missing, and explain the decision in their own words.
If they cannot explain it, they do not own it.
So measure the time the tool removed. Then decide what is supposed to get better because that time exists now.
